ch26.d.V: Potential difference $V$ across the wire; 0 means no field
ch26.d.T: Hotter ions vibrate more and scatter electrons more often (shorter mean free time $\tau$)
ch26.d.A: Cross-sectional area $A$ of the wire (height in the drawing)
ch26.goal.drift: Electrons in a field accelerate between collisions and get a random direction at each one; on average they move at a steady drift velocity $v_d$
ch26.goal.R: Scattering is the origin of resistance: $R = \rho L/A$, with resistivity $\rho$ proportional to the collision rate
ch26.obs.zero: Zero voltage: electrons move fast but in random directions, so the net charge through the cross-section stays at 0
ch26.obs.drift: With a voltage: the path of the outlined electron bends against $\vec E$ between collisions, and the whole population creeps to the left
ch26.obs.count: The slope of the net charge $Q(t)$ through the orange dashed section is the current $I$. Counted from $4\tau$ on, once the drift has built up, $\bar I = \Delta Q/\Delta t$ scatters about the prediction (dashed) and settles onto it
ch26.obs.ohm: Measure at several voltages: the points on the $I$-$V$ chart lie on a straight line through the origin (Ohm's law)
ch26.obs.LA: Double the length: $R$ doubles. Double the cross-section: $R$ halves. Lines of wires measured earlier stay in grey
ch26.obs.T: Higher temperature: more frequent collisions, smaller $v_d$, larger $R$
ch26.assume.speed: Drift speed is hugely exaggerated: in copper $v_d \sim 10^{-4}$ m/s while the electron (Fermi) speed is $\sim 10^{6}$ m/s
ch26.assume.model: Drude model: fixed speed and random direction after each collision, exponentially distributed free times (mean $\tau \propto 1/T$), 2D section, no electron-electron interaction
ch26.assume.units: Each drawn electron stands for many electrons. Its charge is set so that a 4 cm, 2 mm², 300 K wire has 10 Ω. The count uses 8 times as many electrons as are drawn, to cut the thermal noise. The drift builds up as $v_d(1-e^{-t/\tau})$, so $Q/t$ counted from $t = 0$ falls short of the prediction ($-8$ % at 3 s, 300 K). $\bar I$ is therefore $\Delta Q/\Delta t$ counted from $4\tau$ (1 s at 300 K) on: the graph appears after 1 s of counting, the readout $\bar I$ after 2 s. On a small stage the wire is drawn larger beside the $I$-$V$ chart, and a long wire shows only the stretch around the section (wavy cut ends)
ch26.assume.digits: The measured $\bar I$ and $V/\bar I$ print to the first digit of their scatter (counting noise): at the defaults about ±7 mA after 2 s of counting (e.g. 94 mA), about ±1.5 mA after 30 s
ch26.assume.sym: $e$ = 1.60×10⁻¹⁹ C: magnitude of the electron charge, $m$: electron mass, $n$: number of conduction electrons per unit volume. $\tau$: mean free time (average time between collisions), $\tau_{300}$: its value at 300 K (0.25 s). $a$: acceleration of an electron between collisions, $E$: field in the wire, $J = I/A$: current density, $\rho$: resistivity. $\Delta Q$: net charge through the section, $\Delta t$: counting time
ch26.assume.rho: The model's resistivity $\rho$ (5.00×10⁻⁴ Ω·m at 300 K) is about 3×10⁴ times that of copper (1.69×10⁻⁸ Ω·m): it is set so that a 4 cm, 2 mm² wire has 10 Ω, not taken from a real metal
